title: Root: cantāre, cantus (to sing, song) — the buried voice
core: All three come from Latin *cantāre*, "to sing" — and in every one, the singing has become something a voice **does to** a thing: a tone laid over it, a spell sung onto it, a statement sung back and undone. The root is buried, so the family looks like coincidence rather than kinship; what actually survives is the idea that utterance changes status. One heightens what's already there, one binds a listener, one unmakes what was said. Recognising the root won't give you the meanings — but it explains why the spellings rhyme when the senses don't.

words.nuance: From *ad-cantum*, the tone "sung to" a syllable — the accent mark. Alone in this group it needs no voice and no audience: it acts on features and effects (a waistline, a divide, a flaw), and it adds nothing, it only raises the contrast on material that already exists.

From *in-cantāre*, to sing a spell **onto** someone — the only member aimed at a person, and the only one that removes the target's agency. The enchanted party is held and absorbed, not persuaded; where **accentuate** works on a thing and **recant** works on your own past words, this works on somebody else's will.

From *re-cantāre*, to sing back — the only reflexive one: its object is your own earlier statement, and it destroys rather than heightens. Purely a public speech act, usually performed under pressure before the court or church that demanded it, so it carries the coercion the other two never do.

exam_note: The GRE never tests the root — it tests whether *recant* means "retract publicly" (not merely "reconsider") and whether *accentuate* means "heighten what's there" (not "exaggerate" or "add"); the shared "cant" is a red herring the test counts on you over-reading.
